question:
Evaluate the statement: “The Bohr model violates the Heisenberg Uncertainty Principle.”

In the Bohr model of the hydrogen atom, the electron is assumed to move in a circular orbit of definite radius $r_n$ with definite speed $v_n$, hence definite momentum magnitude $p_n=m_ev_n$, and it satisfies the angular momentum condition $m_ev_nr_n=n\hbar$.

For this question, use the uncertainty relation as a provided statement: $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge \dfrac{\hbar}{2}$, where $\Delta x$ is the uncertainty in position along a chosen direction and $\Delta p$ is the uncertainty in the corresponding component of momentum.

Analyse the statement by doing the following:

(i) Explain, using logical reasoning, whether a definite orbit description implies simultaneous definiteness of position and momentum in a way that conflicts with $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge \dfrac{\hbar}{2}$.

(ii) Perform an order-of-magnitude check for the ground orbit using $r_1=a_0=0.529\,\text{\AA}$ and $p_1=\dfrac{\hbar}{r_1}$ from $m_ev_1r_1=\hbar$. Take $\Delta x\sim r_1$ and compare $p_1$ with $\Delta p_{\min}=\dfrac{\hbar}{2\Delta x}$ to comment on consistency at the level of magnitudes.

(iii) Conclude clearly whether the statement should be accepted or rejected, and state the precise sense in which it is true or false.

options.A: True, because the Bohr model assigns a definite orbital radius (position) and a definite momentum $p=m_ev$ simultaneously, which is incompatible with $\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge \dfrac{\hbar}{2}$ if taken literally for an electron at an instant.
options.B: False, because Bohr’s model is fully quantum and therefore automatically includes uncertainty without any conflict.
options.C: True, because in the Bohr model the electron must continuously radiate and fall into the nucleus, so it violates uncertainty.
options.D: False, because the uncertainty principle applies only to the nucleus, not to the electron.
